title: The Effect of Health Insurance Coverage on the Use of Medical Services
research_question: Does gaining or losing health insurance coverage cause changes in the utilization of emergency department and inpatient hospital services among young adults? How large is the effect of insurance coverage on the probability of seeking care, and does it vary by hospital ownership type (public, non-profit, for-profit)?
data_description: The study combines three data sources. First, the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) from 1997 to 2007 provides individual-level information on health insurance coverage type (private, Medicaid, uninsured, other), reasons for losing coverage, school enrollment, and demographics, with the sample restricted to respondents aged 18 to 20 (24,260 observations). Second, a near-census of emergency department visits from Arizona, California, Iowa, New Jersey, and Wisconsin spanning 2004–2007 yields 1,744,394 ED visits among 18- and 19-year-olds, with information on expected payer, age in months, demographics, diagnosis, treatment, and hospital ownership. Third, hospital discharge records from Arizona (2000–2007), California (1990–2006), New York (1990–2006), Iowa (2004–2007), Texas (1999–2003), and Wisconsin (2004–2007) provide 849,610 inpatient admissions among 18- and 19-year-olds. Outcomes include ED visit rates, inpatient admission rates, and insurance coverage shares.
institutional_context: In the United States, many private health insurance contracts cover dependent children only through age 18, with continued coverage available beyond that age primarily for full-time students. As a result, young adults who are not enrolled in school typically lose coverage under their parents' private insurance plans at the end of the month in which they turn 19. This contractual rule generates an abrupt loss of private coverage for a substantial fraction of teenagers immediately upon their 19th birthday—roughly 5 to 8 percentage points overall, and larger among those not in school—without any corresponding offset from Medicaid or other public insurance for most demographic groups (except pregnant women, who often qualify for Medicaid). Young adults are the demographic group most likely to be uninsured, with over half of uninsured non-elderly adults aged 19 to 35, making this setting policy-relevant for understanding coverage expansions.
